item.title: Does Education Protect Workers from Unemployment?
item.dc:creator: Jin Liu
item.description:
Why unemployment by education matters

Unemployment is costly for workers and families, but its burden is not distributed evenly. Education may reduce unemployment risk by giving workers more specialized skills, access to a wider range of occupations, or stronger attachment to employers. It may also separate workers into industries that respond differently to recessions. I ask: How does unemployment vary by education among U.S. adults ages 25-64, and does the gap change when the labor market weakens?

Data and method

I use IPUMS CPS, which harmonizes the monthly Current Population Survey across time. My extract contains April Basic Monthly samples from 2000 through 2025 and the variables YEAR, MONTH, AGE, EDUC, LABFORCE, EMPSTAT, and WTFINL. April gives one comparable cross-section per year and captures the abrupt pandemic disruption in April 2020.

The analysis includes civilians ages 25-64 who are in the labor force. I group education into four levels: less than high school, high school or GED, some college or an associate degree, and a bachelor’s degree or higher. A person is unemployed when the detailed EMPSTAT code is 20-22. The unemployment rate is unemployed people divided by the civilian labor force.

Every estimate uses the final Basic Monthly CPS person weight, WTFINL:

This makes the results describe the U.S. population represented by the CPS rather than the raw observations in the extract. The complete analysis script generates every table and figure.

A persistent education gradient

The first figure establishes whether unemployment rates differ consistently across education groups and shows how all four groups move with the national labor market. Comparing 2000, 2010, 2020, and 2025 also reveals which groups experienced the largest increases during weak labor markets.

In April 2025, the weighted unemployment rate was 6.3% for workers without a high-school diploma and 2.4% for workers with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The same ordering is visible across most years. During the April 2020 shock, the rates rose to 20.8% and 7.9%, respectively. Education therefore marks a persistent difference in unemployment risk, while all groups still move with the wider economy.

The gap changes over the business cycle

The second figure subtracts the unemployment rate for bachelor’s-degree holders from each other group’s rate. This shifts attention from the overall cycle to inequality in unemployment risk. Higher lines during 2010 or 2020 indicate that downturns widened the education gap rather than raising unemployment equally for everyone.

The gap between the least-educated group and bachelor’s-degree holders was 12.9 percentage points in April 2020, compared with 3.9 percentage points in April 2025. The recession-era gap was therefore larger. This comparison shows whether weaker labor markets merely raise unemployment or also concentrate more of the increase among workers with less education.

Education is not simply standing in for age

Education and age are related: older adults have had more time to complete degrees, while younger workers have less labor-market experience. The final figure compares education groups within four age bands in 2025. A consistent education gradient within rows would show that the overall relationship is not solely the result of different age composition.

In 4 of the four age groups, unemployment was higher for adults without a high-school diploma than for adults with a bachelor’s degree or higher. The comparison does not remove every possible difference between workers, but it shows how much of the aggregate education pattern remains after making a simple age adjustment.

Interpretation and takeaway

These figures describe associations, not causal effects. Degree holders differ from other workers in occupation, industry, location, experience, and many other ways. The analysis also uses one month per year, so it describes April conditions rather than an annual average.

The practical lesson is that a single national unemployment rate can conceal large differences in economic security. Read together, the figures show whether more-educated workers experience lower unemployment in ordinary years, whether their advantage expands in downturns, and whether it remains visible within age groups. The main takeaway is that education is related both to the level of unemployment risk and to how strongly workers are exposed when the labor market deteriorates. For workforce agencies, the descriptive evidence can help target job-search assistance and retraining toward less-educated workers, especially during downturns.

Data citation

Flood, Sarah, Miriam King, Renae Rodgers, Steven Ruggles, J. Robert Warren, Daniel Backman, Etienne Breton, Grace Cooper, Julia A. Rivera Drew, Stephanie Richards, David Van Riper, and Kari C. W. Williams. 2025. IPUMS CPS: Version 13.0 [dataset]. Minneapolis, MN: IPUMS. https://doi.org/10.18128/D030.V13.0.

item.title: Which Tech Skills Should I Learn? Evidence from Arbeitnow Jobs
item.description:
A career decision, not just a word count

Learning a new tool takes time. For someone interested in a software, data, or IT job, should the next project use Python, TypeScript, a cloud platform, or something else? Does the board offer remote or entry-level opportunities? Job advertisements offer practical clues. I used Arbeitnow, a Germany-focused job board, to examine skills, role types, work arrangement, and experience level.

From public pages to clean data

On September 21, 2026, my R collection script used rvest to read 100 public listing pages. It saved their HTML and extracted 5000 unique job titles and URLs. Of those titles, 1019 matched a documented software, data, or IT role pattern. Arbeitnow also offers a public job-board API with full descriptions; collecting its paginated feed avoided requesting thousands of individual job pages. The API ended after 29 pages of jobs and supplied 3153 unique descriptions, of which 543 matched the technology-role pattern. 1836 API jobs also appeared in the 100-page HTML snapshot. The two sources are snapshots of the same changing board, so their page lists do not line up exactly.

Code 
library(rvest)
page <- read_html("data/raw/html/page-001.html")
links <- html_elements(page, "a[data-job-item-link]")
job_urls <- html_attr(links, "href")
job_titles <- html_text2(links)

The API pagination helper manages the paced feed requests. The separate analysis script cleans description HTML, removes duplicate URLs, and searches for 20 named technologies. It counts a skill once per job even when the word appears repeatedly. Every skill percentage below divides by the 543 technology jobs with descriptions, not by all HTML listings. The scripts save the cleaned data, tables, and figures; the README gives replication commands. The complete project is in the GitHub repository. Collection used sequential requests with pauses, followed the site’s robots.txt, and used no login or access workaround. Arbeitnow’s API terms ask users to link back to the site.

Which skills appear most often?

Python appears in 187 postings (34.4%), followed by AWS in 114 (21%) and Git in 108 (19.9%). Python and Git appear together in 64 postings. These are mentions, not proof that every employer requires the skill. Percentages do not sum to 100 because one posting can name several technologies.

The overall ranking hides important differences. My title-based groups contain 325 software development, 161 infrastructure or security, and 57 data or machine-learning postings. The two most frequently named skills in each group are:

Work arrangement and experience level

Only 42 of the 543 technology jobs (7.7%) are marked remote. The other 501 have remote = FALSE in the source. That means not marked remote; it does not prove they require full-time office attendance. Remote shares are 9.9% for infrastructure and security, 7.4% for software development, and 3.5% for data and machine learning. The last figure comes from just 2 remote postings, so I would not infer a stable difference between fields.

Experience is another constraint: 198 postings (36.5%) include a senior or lead term in the title, while only 41 (7.6%) include an early-career term. The rest do not state a clear level in the title. An entry-level or remote job seeker should therefore filter listings by those needs before using the overall skill ranking to plan a project.

What should a job seeker do?

If I were targeting data or machine-learning roles, I would build a Python project that queries and analyzes data with SQL: those two skills appear in 49 of 57 data postings and 32 of them, respectively. For software development, I would show Python or TypeScript in a working application. For infrastructure, I would demonstrate deploying and monitoring an application with Kubernetes or a cloud service. These projects provide evidence of ability rather than a list of keywords on a résumé.

The sample has limits. Arbeitnow is one board, many jobs are Germany-focused, and the title filter may miss relevant roles. A technology mentioned in company background or as a preference is still counted. Only 378 of the 543 technology postings mention one of my 20 chosen terms, so the dictionary is incomplete. This analysis measures current advertised language, not hiring outcomes or the return to learning a skill.

Takeaway

The useful lesson is to choose a role and work arrangement first, then use job descriptions to prioritize a small, demonstrable set of skills. Python is the broadest starting point here, but SQL, TypeScript, and Kubernetes matter differently across roles. Remote and early-career openings are a small, specifically labeled part of this sample. Check target postings before investing in a course, and repeat the analysis as listings change.

item.title: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors: The Directions That Stay on Track
item.dc:creator: Jin Liu
item.description:
A complicated name for a visual idea

Imagine drawing arrows on a stretchy sheet. You pull the sheet so that the arrows change length and tilt. Most arrows now point along different lines. But a few special arrows may stay on their original lines, even as they stretch.

Those special arrows capture the idea of eigenvectors. Their eigenvalues tell us how much they are scaled.

The names sound abstract because we often meet them through an equation before seeing the question they answer: Are there directions in which a complicated transformation acts like simple multiplication?

Think of a matrix as a rule for moving arrows

A vector is an arrow described by its coordinates. For example, points one unit right, while points one unit right and one unit up.

A matrix can describe a linear transformation: a rule that preserves vector addition and multiplication by numbers. It can stretch, rotate, reflect, or shear arrows while keeping the origin fixed.

Consider this particular rule:

The entries are instructions: double the first coordinate and add the second; then add the first coordinate to twice the second.

An arrow pointing right, , becomes . It now tilts upward. The transformation changed both its length and its direction.

But try an arrow pointing diagonally northeast:

This arrow gets three times as long but stays on the same line. Therefore, is an eigenvector, with eigenvalue 3.

Now try the other diagonal:

This arrow stays exactly where it was. It is also an eigenvector, with eigenvalue 1.

See the difference

The figure applies the same matrix to three arrows. Dashed arrows show the starting vectors; solid arrows show their transformed versions. Only the last two remain on their original lines.

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

A = np.array([[2, 1], [1, 2]])
vectors = [np.array([1, 0]), np.array([1, 1]), np.array([1, -1])]
titles = ["Ordinary direction", "Eigenvector: eigenvalue 3", "Eigenvector: eigenvalue 1"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 4.6))

for ax, v, title in zip(axes, vectors, titles):
    result = A @ v
    t = np.linspace(-1.5, 3.5, 100)
    ax.plot(t * v[0], t * v[1], color="#dddddd", linewidth=1.5)
    ax.annotate("", xy=result, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#C65319", lw=3))
    ax.annotate("", xy=v, xytext=(0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="#245A81", lw=2,
                                linestyle="--"))
    ax.axhline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
    ax.axvline(0, color="#999999", lw=0.7)
    ax.set(xlim=(-1.5, 3.5), ylim=(-1.5, 3.5),
           xlabel="First coordinate", ylabel="Second coordinate", title=title)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    ax.grid(alpha=0.15)

fig.legend(handles=[Line2D([0], [0], color="#245A81", lw=2,
                          linestyle="--", label="Original vector"),
                    Line2D([0], [0], color="#C65319", lw=3,
                          label="Transformed vector")],
           loc="lower center", ncol=2, frameon=False)
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.09, 1, 1])
plt.show()

The equation is just a comparison

The formal definition is short:

The left side says “apply the matrix.” The right side says “multiply the original vector by a single number.” An eigenvector is a nonzero vector for which those two operations give the same result. That number, (the Greek letter lambda), is the eigenvalue. MIT’s introduction to eigenvalues and eigenvectors

The sign and size matter:

Eigenvalue What happens to the eigenvector?
Its length triples.
It stays unchanged.
Its length halves.
Its length doubles and it points the opposite way.
It collapses to the zero vector.

So “never changes direction” needs a qualification: a negative eigenvalue reverses the arrow, and zero removes its direction entirely. The transformed vector remains on the original line. Also, an eigenvector is not unique in length: works just as well as in our example.

Why this initially feels unintuitive

We usually describe this matrix using horizontal and vertical coordinates. From that viewpoint, it mixes the coordinates together. It seems natural to assume that mixing is unavoidable.

But our example becomes simpler when we use the two diagonal directions instead. Along one diagonal, the rule is “multiply by three.” Along the other, it is “multiply by one.”

Even the ordinary arrow can be broken into those two pieces:

Apply the transformation repeatedly. After applications, the first piece has been multiplied by , while the second is unchanged:

The first piece eventually dwarfs the second, so the resulting arrow points increasingly close to the northeast diagonal. The eigenvectors explain the patterns; the eigenvalues explain how those patterns evolve.

This convenient decomposition works here because the two eigenvectors span the plane. Not every matrix has enough independent eigenvectors for this approach. A 90-degree rotation in the real plane, for example, leaves no nonzero arrow on its original line, so it has no real eigenvectors. MIT lecture notes

An economic interpretation

As a deliberately simplified model, imagine that the two coordinates represent deviations in activity in two sectors. Let our matrix describe how those deviations propagate in one period. These numbers are illustrative assumptions, not estimates from economic data.

The vector represents both sectors moving together. Under this rule, that common movement triples each period. The vector represents one sector rising while the other falls by the same amount. That difference remains unchanged.

Instead of tracking two interacting coordinates, we can track a common movement and an opposing movement. In this toy model, common shocks amplify, while opposing shocks persist. Actual economic conclusions would depend on whether the chosen rule fits the economy, but the mathematical benefit is already visible.

The takeaway

Eigenvectors identify directions where a linear transformation reduces to scaling. Eigenvalues tell us the scale factor, including whether the arrow reverses or disappears.

The surprising part is that a rule that mixes coordinates can become simple when viewed along the right directions. The next time you see , picture an arrow staying on its line—and ask how much it stretches.
